question: What is the meaning of fattening seawater in relation to environmental performance?
description: Fattening seawater refers to the process of desalination, which is the removal of salts and minerals from seawater to make it suitable for drinking or irrigation. This process is often used in areas with limited freshwater resources. In relation to environmental performance, desalination can have both positive and negative impacts. On the positive side, it provides a reliable source of freshwater, which can be crucial for human consumption, agriculture, and industry. However, desalination also has negative environmental impacts, such as high energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and the disposal of brine, a highly concentrated salt byproduct. Therefore, while desalination can contribute to sustainable water management, it is essential to consider and mitigate its environmental impacts.

Accordingly, the EU has developed various approaches in their resources 
strategy. One main approach is to reduce the consumption of primary 
materials, by increasing recycling rates, which is associated with Cir­
cular Economy (CE). CE stands in contrast to linear economy, which 
builds upon a “take-make-waste” approach (Mining, 2015). Linear 
economy began during the industrial revolution, where long-term 
damage was caused through exploitation of resources and ignorance 
of the environmental limits (Prieto-Sandoval et al., 2018). Within CE 
models, materials and elements embedded in buildings act as material 
banks (secondary raw materials) for new buildings, by staying in the 
loop and not creating waste (Hopkinson et al., 2018). Therefore, the aim 
should be to reuse or recycle the materials from the stock, which is a 
strategy entitled Urban Mining – a concept within CE. Urban Mining is 
promoting a systematic reuse of anthropogenic materials from urban 
areas. In contrast to usual recycling, Urban Mining includes, apart from 
mining of waste, also the exploration and observation of materials in 
buildings and infrastructures (Klinglmair and Fellner, 2010). However, 
the realization of Urban Mining strategies is still a challenging task, due 
to the lack of information about materials and substances embedded in 
buildings (Brunner, 2011). New construction projects are usually well 
documented; however, this is not the case for the building stock 
(Bergsdal et al., 2007). As buildings have a long lifespan, they are 
confronted with many adaptations throughout their life-cycle, thus the 
original material composition might change (M´equignon and Haddou, 
2014) and does not comply with the actual state of the building. Several 
studies were conducted to identify the urban stock, whereby mainly the 
top-down and bottom-up approaches were used. Within the top-down 
approach the balance between the amount of materials entering the 
system (e.g. use phase of a building) and the amount exiting the system 
are estimated (Cheng et al., 2018). The bottom-up approach is based on 
inventories of materials and uses parameters such as the period of 
construction or building height for upscaling (Oezdemir et al., 2017). 
The main problem with both approaches is, that they do not deliver 
accurate information about the material stock, since the estimates are 
too general, neglecting the fact that every building is unique and com­
prises of different materials. Most studies categorize buildings regarding 
their function (residential, non-residential), size (small or large build­
ing) and their load-bearing structure (Koutamanis et al., 2018). Schebek 
et al. (2017) assessed the material stocks of non-residential buildings 
through analysis of spatial data and examination of single buildings (mix 
of bottom-up and top-down approach). The study provides area-wide 
information on material stocks including the function and age-class of 
buildings. Deetman et al. (2020) created a model on the global building 
stock and construction materials demand based on the inflows and 
outflows of urban building materials. Other studies, such as Xue et al. 
(2017) and Kleemann et al. (2017) use data from GIS (geographical 
information system) for estimation the Urban Mining opportunities on 
city or regional level. By coupling GIS data with street photographs, 
Kleemann et al. (2016) tried to gather more detailed information such as 
cladding materials or the type of roof. High-tech approaches for iden­
tification of materials was tested through image-based recognition of 
point-clouds, whereby the surface materials of buildings were detected 
through machine learning algorithms (Yang et al., 2016). 
Various tools and methods are used to support the implementation of 
sustainable development into the AEC (Architecture, Engineering and 
Construction) sector (Alwan et al., 2017), such as Life Cycle Assessment 
(LCA), Energy Certificates, Material Flow Analysis (MFA), Environ­
mental Product Declarations (EPD) etc. Especially LCA has found a 
broad application, as it assesses buildings and built environment’s 
environmental impacts throughout the whole life-cycle (Hossain and 
Ng, 2018).
